paragraphs.heading: Inputs that give zero
paragraphs.text: A zero of a function, also called a root, is an input that makes the output equal 0. Put another way, it is a solution of the equation f(x) = 0. A root of a polynomial is simply a zero of the matching polynomial function. For example, f(x) = x² − 5 x + 6 factors as (x − 2) (x − 3), and its roots are 2 and 3, since f(2) and f(3) both come out to 0.

paragraphs.heading: Where a graph meets the axis
paragraphs.text: When a function takes real numbers to real numbers, you can see its zeros on its graph. They are the x-coordinates of the points where the graph touches the x-axis. Such a point (x, 0) is also called an x-intercept.

paragraphs.heading: Every equation is a root problem
paragraphs.text: Any equation in an unknown x can be rearranged as f(x) = 0 by moving all of its terms to the left-hand side. The solutions of the equation are then exactly the zeros of f. So studying the zeros of functions and studying the solutions of equations are one and the same task.

paragraphs.heading: How many roots
paragraphs.text: The fundamental theorem of algebra says a non-zero polynomial has at most as many roots as its degree. If you count complex roots, each as many times as its multiplicity, the number of roots equals the degree exactly. When the coefficients are real, any non-real roots come in conjugate pairs.

paragraphs.heading: Odd and even degree
paragraphs.text: If a real polynomial's degree is odd, the count of its real roots is odd too, counting multiplicities; if the degree is even, the count is even. So an odd-degree real polynomial always has at least one real root, but an even-degree one may have none. The reason is the intermediate value theorem: polynomial functions are continuous, so a value that changes from negative to positive must pass through zero on the way.

paragraphs.heading: Finding roots in practice
paragraphs.text: Vieta's formulas tie a polynomial's coefficients to the sums and products of its roots. Every polynomial of degree 4 or less can have its roots written out algebraically from its coefficients. For approximating roots there are many methods, the best being Newton's method, and polynomials have their own faster algorithms that can find all roots or all real roots.

paragraphs.heading: Sets of zeros
paragraphs.text: Gather every zero of a function together and you get its zero set. In algebraic geometry, an affine algebraic set is where the zero sets of several polynomials overlap, and a zero set there is sometimes called a zero locus. The unit m-sphere in R ^(m+1), for example, is the zero set of the function f(x) = ‖ x ‖² − 1.
